Moral Hazard and Incentives

This scene designs a contract when the boss cannot watch the work. A flat wage alone gives no reason to work hard.

Pay must hang on the outcome. Good results need a bonus on top. Two conditions must hold at once. Working hard must beat slacking off. And the job must be worth taking at all. The less the worker fears risk, the gentler the bonus slope. It is a tug-of-war between sharing risk and pushing effort.

For example, you run a 🏪 snack shop and leave a part-timer alone. You cannot see how hard they work. So you do not fix the wage. On days the shop earns more 💰 money, you pay a bonus. Then the part-timer works hard on their own.

With the same parameters but α=1\alpha = 1α=1 (a risk-neutral agent), find the optimal contract and show the risk premium is zero.

Incentive compatibility still demands a wage gap — why does the cost equal full insurance anyway?

wL=uL=16.667,wH=uH=33.333w_L = u_L = 16.667, \qquad w_H = u_H = 33.333wL​=uL​=16.667,wH​=uH​=33.333
C1=0.8×33.333+0.2×16.667=30=uˉ+cC_1 = 0.8 \times 33.333 + 0.2 \times 16.667 = 30 = \bar u + cC1​=0.8×33.333+0.2×16.667=30=uˉ+c
Show proof

  1. The utility spread (uL,uH)=(16.667,33.333)(u_L, u_H) = (16.667, 33.333)(uL​,uH​)=(16.667,33.333) is pinned down by IC and IR regardless of α\alphaα. With α=1\alpha = 1α=1, u(w)=wu(w) = wu(w)=w, so wages equal utilities: wL=16.667w_L = 16.667wL​=16.667, wH=33.333w_H = 33.333wH​=33.333.

  2. The expected wage is C1=0.8×33.333+0.2×16.667=30C_1 = 0.8 \times 33.333 + 0.2 \times 16.667 = 30C1​=0.8×33.333+0.2×16.667=30. The full-insurance cost (uˉ+c)1=30(\bar u + c)^1 = 30(uˉ+c)1=30 matches it, so the risk premium is zero.

  3. Why: a risk-neutral agent suffers no utility loss from wage variation. Translating the IC-mandated utility spread into a wage spread costs nothing, so the principal buys incentives at the full-insurance expected cost — the pay slope is steep but risk-sharing costs zero.
